question: Two parallel glass plates separated by a small gap x are dipped in a liquid of surface tension T, density ρ. If the angle of contact is θ then the height up to which the liquid rises is
solution:
Consider two large parallel vertical glass plates separated by a small distance x .

The width of each plate along the horizontal direction be L .

Let the liquid of density of the liquid be $\rho$, the surface tension be T rises to a height h between the plates.

The contact angle with the glass plates be $\theta$.

The liquid column of height $h$ held between the plates is in static equilibrium under two vertical forces.

The upward vertical force exerted by surface tension along the contact line on both plates.

The downward gravitational force (weight) of the elevated liquid column.

The liquid is in contact with two vertical plates, each having a contact line of length $L$.

So, total length of the contact line along both plates is $L_{\text{eff}} = L + L = 2L$

The surface tension force per unit length is $T$, acting along the tangent to the liquid meniscus at an angle $\theta$ to the vertical glass surface.

The vertically upward component of the surface tension force per unit length is $T_y = T \cos \theta$

Therefore, the total upward force $F_{\text{up}}$ acting on the liquid column is $F_{\text{up}} = (2L) \cdot T \cos \theta = 2TL \cos \theta$

The volume of the liquid column raised between the plates is $V = x \cdot L \cdot h$

The mass of this liquid column is $m = \rho \cdot V = \rho x L h$

The downward force due to gravity (weight $W$) is $W = mg = \rho x L h g$

For static equilibrium along vertical direction,

F_{\text{up}} = W

\Rightarrow 2TL \cos \theta = \rho x L h g

\Rightarrow 2T \cos \theta = x \rho g h

\Rightarrow h = $\frac{2T \cos \theta}{x \rho g}$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

question: A straight cylindrical glass rod of diameter $d_1$ is inserted coaxially into a glass tube of inner diameter $d_2$ and such that the separation between them is capillary $[(d_2 - d_1) \ll d_1, d_2]$. The whole set up is vertically placed in contact with water surface (surface tension = $T$, density = $\rho$). If the capillary rise be $h$, then
solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \text { Inner rod diameter }=d_1 \Rightarrow \text { Radius } r_1=\frac{d_1}{2} \\ & \text { Outer tube inner diameter }=d_2 \Rightarrow \text { Radius } r_2=\frac{d_2}{2}\end{aligned}$

The liquid rises to a height $h$ in the annular gap between the outer surface of the inner rod and the inner surface of the outer tube.

For pure water on clean glass, the contact angle is $\theta = 0^{\circ}$, so $\cos\theta = 1$.

Inner contact line along the outer surface of the cylindrical rod of circumference $\pi d_1$.

Outer contact line along the inner surface of the cylindrical tube of circumference $\pi d_2$.

The total upward force due to surface tension acting on the elevated liquid column is:

F_{\text{up}} = T(\pi d_1)\cos 0^{\circ} + T(\pi d_2)\cos 0^{\circ}

F_{\text{up}} = \pi T(d_1 + d_2)

The cross-sectional area of the annular region between the rod and the tube is,

A = $\frac{\pi}{4}$d_2^2 - $\frac{\pi}{4}$d_1^2 = $\frac{\pi}{4}($d_2^2 - d_1^2)

A = $\frac{\pi}{4}($d_2 - d_1)(d_2 + d_1)

The volume of the liquid column raised up to height $h$ is $V = A \cdot h = \frac{\pi}{4}(d_2 - d_1)(d_2 + d_1)h$

The downward weight of this liquid column is $W = \rho V g = \rho \left[\frac{\pi}{4}(d_2 - d_1)(d_2 + d_1)h\right] g$

In equilibrium along vertical direction,

F_{up} = W \Rightarrow \pi T (d_1 + d_2) = $\frac{\pi}{4} \rho$g h (d_2 - d_1)(d_2 + d_1)

h = $\frac{4T}{\rho g (d_2 - d_1)}$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

question: A water droplet starts falling from rest from a height h and acquires the terminal speed just before reaching the ground. If g (acceleration due to gravity) is assumed to be constant and radius of the drop is r, the work done by air drag is. (The co-efficient of viscosity of air is η)
solution:
A spherical droplet of radius r and density $\rho_{\mathrm{w}}$ falling through air of density $\rho_{\text {air }}$ and viscosity $\eta$.

The forces acting on the droplet are downward gravitational force

W = mg = \$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right) g

The upward buoyant force acting on the sphere is,

F_B = \rho_{\text{air}} V g = \$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_{\text{air}}\right) g

Upward viscous drag force given by Stokes' law

F_v = 6\pi \eta r v

At terminal velocity $v_t$, the acceleration is zero, so the net force is zero.

W = F_B + F_v

\$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right) g = \$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_{\text{air}}\right) g + 6\pi \eta r v_t

$\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 (\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}}) g = 6\pi \eta r v_t

v_t = 4\pi r^3 \$left[\frac{(\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}}) g}{3 \times 6\pi \eta r}\right] = \frac{2 r^2 g (\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}})}{9\eta}$

$v_t^2=4 r^4 g^2 \frac{\left(\rho_w-\rho_{\text {air }}\right)^2}{81 \eta^2}$

Using the work-energy theorem the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy.

W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i

The droplet starts from rest from height $h$, so initial kinetic energy is $K_i = 0$.

Just before reaching the ground, it achieves terminal speed $v_t$, so the final kinetic energy is;

K_f = $\frac{1}{2}$m v_t^2 = $\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right) v_t^2

The forces doing work during the downward vertical displacement $h$ are gravity, buoyancy, and the air drag,

W_{\text{net}} = W_g + W_B + W_{\text{drag}}

Where work done by gravity is $W_g = +mgh = +\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_w\right)gh$

Work done by buoyant force is $W_B = -F_B\,h = -\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_{\text{air}}\right)gh$

Work done by air drag is $W_{\text{drag}}$

Using the work energy expression $W_g + W_B + W_{\text{drag}} = K_f$

\$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right)gh - \$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_{\text{air}}\right)gh + W_{\text{drag}} = $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right)v_t^2

W_{\text{drag}} = $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right)v_t^2 - $\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3(\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}})gh

Substituting $v_t^2 = 4r^4 g^2 \frac{(\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}})^2}{81\eta^2}$:

W_{\text{drag}} = $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w\right)\left[4r^4 g^2 $\frac{(\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}})^2}{81\eta^2}\right] - \frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w gh \left(1 - $\frac{\rho_{\text{air}}}{\rho_w}\right)$

W_{\text{drag}} = $\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3 \rho_w g\$left[\frac{2r^4 g}{81\eta^2}(\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}})^2 - h \left(1 - $\frac{\rho_{\text{air}}}{\rho_w}\right)\right]$

Therefore, the work done by air drag is $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_w g \left[\frac{2r^4 g}{81\eta^2}(\rho_w - \rho_{\text{air}})^2 - h \left(1 - $\frac{\rho_{\text{air}}}{\rho_w}\right)\right]. Thus, the correct option is (A).

$

question: A vertical glass capillary tube of radius r open at both ends contains some water (surface tension T and density ρ). If L be the length of the water column, then
solution:
The vertical capillary tube is open at both ends and holds a suspended column of water of length L.

Downward gravitational force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{g}}=\mathrm{W}=$ weight of the water column.

Upward force due to surface tension along the upper meniscus $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{S} 1}$

Upward force due to surface tension along the lower meniscus $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{S} 2}$

The capillary tube is cylindrical with internal radius r.

So, its cross-sectional area is $\mathrm{A}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2$

Volume of the water column is $\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{L}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~L}$

Mass of the water column is $\mathrm{m}=\rho \mathrm{V}=\rho \pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~L}$

So, the downward weight of the water column is,

\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~L} \rho \mathrm{~g}

Water wets glass completely, so, the angle of contact is $\theta \approx 0^\circ$.

For each meniscus, the liquid surface meets the tube wall along a circular perimeter of length $2\pi r$.

So, the upward vertical force exerted on the upper meniscus is $F_{S1} = T(2\pi r)\cos 0^\circ = 2\pi rT$

And, the upward vertical force exerted on the lower meniscus is $F_{S1} = T(2\pi r)\cos 0^\circ = 2\pi rT$

Therefore, the total upward force exerted by surface tension at both ends is,

F_{\text{up}} = F_{S1} + F_{S2} = 2\pi rT + 2\pi rT = 4\pi rT

For the vertical column of water to remain supported in static equilibrium,

W = F_{\text{up}} \Rightarrow \pi r^2 L\rho g = 4\pi rT

\Rightarrow rL\rho g = 4T

\Rightarrow L = $\frac{4T}{r\rho g}$

Therefore, the length of water column is $\frac{4T}{r\rho g}$. Thus, the correct option is (A).

question: A thread is tied slightly loose to a wire frame as shown in the figure. And the frame is dipped into a soap solution and taken out. The frame is completely covered with the film. When the portion A is punctured with a pin, the thread :
options: either (a) or (b) depending on size of A w.r.t. B
solution:
The wire frame has a loose thread tied across it dividing the interior into two regions, region A and region B .

A soap film is formed over both regions A and B.

In this state, the soap film in region A exerts a surface tension pull on the thread towards region A, and the soap film in region B exerts an equal surface tension pull towards region B.

Hence, the net surface tension force on the thread is balanced, and the thread remains loose in its arbitrary position.

When region A is pricked with a pin, the soap film in region A breaks and completely disappears. As a result, the pull on the thread from side A becomes zero. However, the soap film in region B is still in contact with every element of the thread and exerts pull.

The surface tension tries to minimize their surface area to achieve minimum surface energy ( $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{T} \cdot$ Area).

To minimize the area of the remaining film in region B , the film pulls the flexible thread inward into region B as much as possible, away from region A.

As the film in region B contracts to make its surface area as small as possible, it pulls the thread tight, pulling it inward into B.

A curve bending away from an observer appears concave when viewed from that side.

Since the thread is pulled towards B and curves away from A , the boundary curves inwards into region B , making it concave towards A and convex towards B.

Thus, the correct option is (B).

question: A tiny air bubble of radius r in water is at a depth h below the water surface at some instant. If $p_0$ is atmospheric pressure and d and T are the density and surface tension of water respectively, the pressure inside the bubble will be :
solution:
The free surface of the water is exposed to atmospheric pressure $\mathrm{p}_0$. At a depth h below the surface, the hydrostatic pressure of the water $\mathrm{p}_{\text {water }}$ is the sum of the atmospheric pressure and the pressure exerted by the column of water of height $h$.

$\mathrm{p}_{\text {water }}=\mathrm{p}_0+\mathrm{hdg}$

Here, d is the density of water and g is the acceleration due to gravity.

question: The lower end of a capillary tube of radius r cm is placed vertically in water. If S is the surface tension of water, the heat dissipated due to capillary rise is given by $\frac{n \pi S^n}{\rho g}$. Find $n$.
solution:
$The inner radius of the capillary tube be r .

The surface tension of water be $S$.

The density of water be $\rho$.

The acceleration due to gravity be g .

The contact angle between water and the glass tube be $\theta_{\mathrm{c}}$.

For pure water and clean glass, $\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \approx 0^{\circ}$, so $\cos \theta_{\mathrm{c}}=1$.

At the contact line of circumference $2 \pi \mathrm{r}$, the upward vertical force exerted by surface tension is:

\mathrm{F}_{\text {up }}=(2 \pi \mathrm{r}) \mathrm{S} \cos \theta_{\mathrm{c}}=2 \pi \mathrm{rS}

As water rises to an equilibrium height $h$, the weight of water column is,

\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg}=\left(\rho \pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~h}\right) \mathrm{g}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~h} \rho \mathrm{~g}

The upward surface tension force balances the downward weight of the elevated liquid column:

2 \pi \mathrm{rS}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~h} \rho \mathrm{~g}

h = $\frac{2S}{\rho g r}$

During the rise of the liquid column, the boundary of the meniscus moves upward by a vertical distance equal to $h$.

The upward force of surface tension $F_{\text{up}} = 2\pi r S$ remains constant throughout the upward movement.

Therefore, the total work done by surface tension is:

W_{\text{ST}} = F_{\text{up}} \times h = (2\pi r S)h

W_{\text{ST}} = (2\pi r S)\$left(\frac{2S\rho}{g\,r}\right) = \frac{4\pi S^2}{\rho g}$

The total mass of the raised liquid column is $m = \pi r^2 h\rho$

Since the water column is uniform, its center of mass is elevated to a height of $\frac{h}{2}$ above the free water surface.

Thus, the gain in gravitational potential energy of the raised water column is

\Delta U = mg\$left(\frac{h}{2}\right) = (\pi$r^2 h\rho g)\$left(\frac{h}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}(\pi$r^2 h\rho g)h

Using $\pi r^2 h\rho g = 2\pi r S$:

\Delta U = $\frac{1}{2}($2\pi r S)h = \pi r S h

Substituting $h = \frac{2S\rho}{gr}$,

\Delta U = (\pi r S)\$left(\frac{2S}{\rho g r}\right) = \frac{2\pi S^2}{\rho g}$

By the work-energy theorem, the total work done by the surface tension force goes into increasing the gravitational potential energy of the liquid column and into thermal energy.

\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{ST}}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\mathrm{Q}

The heat dissipated is $\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{ST}}-\Delta \mathrm{U}=\frac{4 \pi \mathrm{~S}^2}{\rho \mathrm{~g}}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~S}^2}{\rho \mathrm{~g}}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~S}^2}{\rho \mathrm{~g}}$

\$mathrm{Q}=\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi \mathrm{~S}^{\mathrm{n}}}{\rho \mathrm{~g}}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~S}^2}{\rho \mathrm{~g}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=$2

Therefore, the value of n is 2 .

$

Therefore, the value of n is 2 .

$

q: A number of little droplets of a liquid of surface tension $T$, density $\rho$, all of same radius $r$, combine to form a single drop of radius $R$. If the total energy released in this process is converted into kinetic energy of the bigger drop, velocity of the bigger drop is $\sqrt{\frac{K T(R-r)}{\operatorname{Rr} \rho}}$. Find the value of $K$.
question: A number of little droplets of a liquid of surface tension $T$, density $\rho$, all of same radius $r$, combine to form a single drop of radius $R$. If the total energy released in this process is converted into kinetic energy of the bigger drop, velocity of the bigger drop is $\sqrt{\frac{K T(R-r)}{\operatorname{Rr} \rho}}$. Find the value of $K$.
solution:
Let N be the number of identical small droplets of radius r that coalesce to form a single larger drop of radius R.

Since the liquid is incompressible, the total volume remains conserved, $V_{\text{initial}} = V_{\text{final}}$

N\$left(\frac{4}{3}\pi$r^3\right) = $\frac{4}{3}\pi$R^3

\Rightarrow Nr^3 = R^3 \Rightarrow N = $\frac{R^3}{r^3}$

The total mass M of the formed bigger drop is $M = \rho V_{\text{final}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\rho$

Surface energy of a spherical liquid droplet of radius a is $U_s = T \cdot A = T(4\pi a^2)$

Total initial surface energy of N small droplets:

U_i = N(4\pi r^2 T) = \$left(\frac{R^3}{r^3}\right)($4\pi r^2 T) = 4\pi R^3 T\$left(\frac{1}{r}\right)$

Final surface energy of the single combined drop $U_f = 4\pi R^2 T = 4\pi R^3 T $\$left(\frac{1}{R}\right)

Total surface energy released in the process,

\Delta U = U_i - U_f = 4\pi R^3 T \left( \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{R} \right) = 4\pi R^3 T \left( \frac{R-r}{Rr} \right)

It is given that the released surface energy is converted into kinetic energy of the bigger drop.

\frac{1}{2} M v^2 = \Delta U

Substituting the mass $M = $\frac{4}{3}\pi$R^3 \rho$ and the expression for $\Delta U$:

$\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{4}{3}\pi$R^3 \rho \right) v^2 = 4\pi R^3 T \left( $\frac{R-r}{Rr} \right)$

\left( $\frac{2}{3}\pi$R^3 \rho \right) v^2 = 4\pi R^3 T \left( $\frac{R-r}{Rr} \right)$

$\frac{2}{3} \rho$v^2 = 4T \left( $\frac{R-r}{Rr} \right)$

v^2 = 4 \times $\frac{3}{2} \cdot$T \left[ $\frac{(R-r)}{\rho Rr} \right] = \frac{6T(R-r)}{\rho Rr}$

v = $\sqrt{\frac{6T(R-r)}{\rho Rr}} = \sqrt{\frac{KT(R-r)}{\rho Rr}} \Rightarrow$K = 6

Therefore, the value of K is 6.

$

q: There is an air bubble of radius $R$ inside a drop of water of radius $3 R$. Find the ratio of gauge pressure at point A to the gauge pressure at point B.
question: There is an air bubble of radius $R$ inside a drop of water of radius $3 R$. Find the ratio of gauge pressure at point A to the gauge pressure at point B.
solution:
The radius of outer spherical water drop is $\mathrm{R}_{\text {drop }}=3 \mathrm{R}$ which is surrounded by outside air at atmospheric pressure $\mathrm{P}_0$.

Inside this water drop, there is an air bubble of radius $\mathrm{R}_{\text {bubble }}=\mathrm{R}$.

Gauge pressure \left(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{g}}\right)$ at any point is $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{g}}=\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{P}_0$, where P is the absolute pressure at that point.

Let T be the surface tension of water.

A spherical liquid drop in air has a single liquid-air interface of radius $\mathrm{R}_{\text {drop }}=3 \mathrm{R}$.

Across a curved spherical liquid surface of radius $r$, the excess pressure on the concave side (inside the liquid drop) compared to the convex side (outside air) is

\Delta P = $\frac{2T}{r}$

For the water drop of radius $3R$, using excess pressure formula;

P_B - P_0 = $\frac{2T}{3R}$

Therefore, the gauge pressure at point B is

P_{g,B} = P_B - P_0 = $\frac{2T}{3R}$

The air bubble of radius $R$ is inside the liquid. It forms an interface between the water (outside the bubble) and the air (inside the bubble).

The concave side of this interface is inside the air bubble, so the pressure inside the bubble ($P_A$) is greater than the pressure in the surrounding water ($P_B$),

P_A - P_B = $\frac{2T}{R_{\text{bubble}}} = \frac{2T}{R}$

P_A = P_B + $\frac{2T}{R} = \left($P_0 + $\frac{2T}{3R}\right) +$2TR = P_0 + $\frac{8T}{3R}$

Therefore, the gauge pressure at point A is,

P_{g,A} = P_A - P_0 = $\frac{8T}{3R}$

Hence, the ratio of the gauge pressure at point A to the gauge pressure at point B is,

$\frac{P_{g,A}}{P_{g,B}} = \frac{\frac{8T}{3R}}{\frac{2T}{3R}} = \frac{8}{2} =$4

Thus, the ratio of gauge pressure at point A to the gauge pressure at point B is 4.

$

q: A thin square plate of side $\mathbf{l}=\mathbf{1 0 ~ c m}$ is dragged with constant velocity $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{3 c m} \boldsymbol{/} \mathbf{s}$ in caster oil of thickness $\mathbf{d}=2 \mathrm{~mm}$. Find the horizontal force (in N ) required to move it, if $\eta=150$ poise.
question: A thin square plate of side $\mathbf{l}=\mathbf{1 0 ~ c m}$ is dragged with constant velocity $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{3 c m} \boldsymbol{/} \mathbf{s}$ in caster oil of thickness $\mathbf{d}=2 \mathrm{~mm}$. Find the horizontal force (in N ) required to move it, if $\eta=150$ poise.
solution:
The side length of thin square plate is l which is moving horizontally at a constant velocity $\mathrm{v}=3 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$.

The thickness of layer of castor oil is d.

Because the plate moves at a constant velocity, its acceleration is zero. By Newton's first law, the external applied horizontal force F must balance the viscous drag force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}$ exerted by the oil on the surface of the plate,

\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}

According to Newton's law of viscosity, the shear stress $\tau$ between parallel fluid layers in laminar flow is proportional to the velocity gradient perpendicular to the flow direction, $\tau=\eta \frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dy}}$, where $\eta$ is the dynamic coefficient of viscosity.

Assuming a linear velocity profile across the thin layer of thickness d ,

At the fixed bottom surface $(\mathrm{y}=0)$ the velocity of flow is $\mathrm{v}=0$ as for no-slip condition.

At the plate surface $\mathrm{z}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$ (because the plate is symmetrically placed at center) the velocity of flow is equal to the velocity of plate $\mathrm{v}=3 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$.

So, the velocity gradient is $\frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dy}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}-0}{\mathrm{~d} / 2}=\frac{2 \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{d}}$

The shear stress acting over the contact area A of the plate is $\tau=\frac{2 \eta \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{d}}$

The total horizontal viscous drag force is $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}=\tau \times \mathrm{A}=\frac{2 \eta \mathrm{Av}}{\mathrm{d}}$

Therefore, the required horizontal force is

F = 2F_v = $\frac{2 \times 2\eta A v}{d} = \frac{4\eta A v}{d}$

The side length of the square plate is $l = 10\ \text{cm} = 0.1\ \text{m}$

So, surface area of the square plate is

A = l^2 = (0.1\ \text{m})^2 = 0.01\ \text{m}^2 = 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2

Velocity of the plate is

v = 3\ \text{cm/s} = 3 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m/s} = 0.03\ \text{m/s}

Thickness of the oil layer

d = 2\ \text{mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}

The coefficient of viscosity is $[1\ \text{poise} = 0.1\ \text{N} \cdot \text{s}/\text{m}^2 = 0.1\ \text{Pa} \cdot \text{s}]$

\eta = 150\ \text{poise} = 150 \times 0.1\ \text{N} \cdot \text{s}/\text{m}^2 = 15\ \text{N} \cdot \text{s}/\text{m}^2

Substituting the values,

F = $\frac{4 \times 15 \times 10^{-2} \times (3 \times 10^{-2})}{2 \times 10^{-3}}$

F = $\frac{180 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{18}{2} =$9\ \text{N}

Therefore, the horizontal force required to move the plate is $9\ \text{N}$.
